“Then you will remain uncertain until morning.”

The threat was not in his voice. That made it worse.

A clock began to strike somewhere deep in the house. The sound traveled through the walls, each chime arriving from a different direction. Five. Six. Seven.

But the clock in the gallery showed ten minutes past six.

I looked at Kreel.

He had noticed it too. His eyes had gone to the ceiling, not the clock.

A concealed mechanism clicked behind the portrait.

Vale’s face had gone pale.

“Dinner at seven,” he repeated. “Until then, I suggest you make yourselves useful by remembering precisely where you were when the lights fail.”

No one laughed.

Outside, thunder rolled over the island. The glass roof flashed white, and for an instant the unfinished house in the portrait seemed to stand behind us, its scaffold crowded with faceless men.

Then the lights steadied, the clock stopped, and somewhere below our feet a door closed.

chapters.name: Dinner Under Glass
chapters.content:
The dining room was built over the western drop, its three outer walls made of glass.

In daylight, I imagined, the arrangement might have seemed triumphant. At night it made the sea feel like an accomplice. Black water climbed the panes, broke apart under the rain, and vanished again. Each flash of lightning showed the cliff below in brief white slices, as if the island were being photographed by someone who could not hold the camera steady.

There were eight places at the table, though only seven of us sat down.

Vale occupied the head, beneath a brass chandelier shaped like a cluster of inverted compasses. Celia sat on his right, Adrian on his left. Kreel took the chair opposite Celia. Orr sat beside me, his canvas satchel tucked beneath the table, and Agnes served from a sideboard without joining us.

The eighth place remained empty.

I noticed Vale watching me notice it.

“An old habit,” he said.

“Waiting for someone?”

“Expecting one.”

Celia gave a short, humorless laugh. “He means Mother.”

The room changed. It was not a dramatic change. No one moved, and the rain continued to strike the glass with the same hard persistence. But the empty chair acquired a person. A woman who had once sat there, perhaps with her hands folded beside the silver, perhaps looking out at the same black water.

Vale’s fingers tightened around his cane.

“Your mother has been dead for twenty-nine years,” he said.

“No,” Celia replied. “That’s the convenient word for it.”

Agnes set down a tureen of soup. She did it carefully, as though the porcelain might hear.

Vale lifted his spoon. “We will eat before we exhume the family.”

“We might as well start with the island,” Celia said. “That’s what you intend to exhume next.”

Adrian leaned back, one hand already around his wineglass. “Could we not wait until the fish?”

“The fish is dead already,” Celia said. “It has no further claim on our patience.”

Vale looked toward me. “Celia believes I have invited you here to provide moral authority for a business decision.”

“I believe you invited her because you enjoy making a room uncomfortable,” Celia said. “The moral authority is incidental.”

“I invited Mara because she has a particular expertise.”

“Locked rooms?”

“False rooms.”

That quieted them, though not for long.

Agnes served me soup. It smelled of leeks, pepper, and something medicinal underneath. I tasted it and found it good. The ordinary quality of the meal unsettled me more than if it had been bad. Someone had planned the courses, polished the silver, folded the napkins into sharp white triangles. The house could contain secret passages, disputed graves, and a man who had received threats of disappearance, yet dinner still arrived on schedule.

A clock struck somewhere behind the walls.

One note. Then another, distant and distorted. A third seemed to come from beneath us.

Adrian looked up. “There it is again.”

Kreel glanced toward the ceiling. His face remained composed, but his spoon stopped halfway to his mouth.

Vale said, “The clocks are being repaired.”

“All of them?” I asked.

“Some of them.”

“By whom?”

“By the same people who failed to repair them the first time.”

Adrian drank his wine. “That means Simon.”

Kreel lowered his spoon. “It means the house is old.”

“It means you’ve been rebuilding the place for thirty years and it still tells time like a drunk.”

“I have restored the systems Vale asked me to restore.”

“Not the ones he asked you to hide?”

Celia’s words fell neatly between them.

Vale put down his spoon. “We are not discussing the development tonight.”

“We are discussing nothing else,” she said. “The plans are on your desk. The surveyors arrived last week. The marina company has already sent representatives to the mainland. You expect us to sit here and pretend the future of Blackwater is not being auctioned under the table.”

“It is not being auctioned.”

“Then why does the offer expire Monday?”

Adrian’s head turned sharply. He looked from Celia to his father. “What offer?”

Celia ignored him. “The island is not a collection of picturesque ruins you can package for people with yachts. The marsh is protected. The west cliff is unstable. The old drainage tunnels are still active.”

“Which is precisely why the development would fund proper repairs,” Kreel said.

His voice was calm, almost kind. That made it more effective than anger would have been.

“The company proposes a limited resort,” he continued. “Thirty-six rooms, a small marina, restoration of the chapel road, employment for local tradesmen. Blackwater is deteriorating. Sentiment will not hold up the cliff.”

“Concrete will,” Celia said.

“Concrete, drainage, reinforcement, and money. All things you have not supplied.”

She looked at me. “He says that as though I have been given a budget.”

“You have been given an allowance.”

“An allowance is not a budget. It’s a leash.”

Adrian gave a brittle laugh. “Some of us would be grateful for a leash.”

Celia turned on him. “You’ve had money every time you asked.”

“I’ve had loans.”

“Because you spend everything.”

“Because Father keeps threatening to cut me off.”

“Because you keep making it necessary.”

Adrian’s face had gone pale beneath his fair hair. The wineglass trembled in his hand. I remembered the first time I had seen a suspect’s hand shake at an interview table. Fear was not always evidence of guilt. Sometimes it was only fear of being seen accurately.

“How much?” he asked Vale.

Vale looked at him. “Not here.”

“You said you’d cover the bank by Friday.”

“I said I would consider it.”

“You said—”

“I said no.”

The storm struck the house then. A hard blast of wind made the glass wall groan. Somewhere above us, a metal structure clanged and swung. Agnes caught the edge of the sideboard before the tureen slid.

No one spoke until the sound passed.

Then Orr said, “How many people died during the construction?”

Vale’s eyes moved to him.

Orr had barely touched his soup. He was young enough to look out of place among the old money and old resentments at the table, but he had a historian’s patience. He did not rush to fill silence. He let it show what it contained.

“I have seen five names,” he said. “Six, if Gabriel Rusk is included. Seven if Livia Vale’s disappearance is counted as something other than an accident.”

Adrian’s glass stopped halfway to his mouth.

Vale’s face hardened. “You have been reading sensational pamphlets.”

“I’ve been reading contractor accounts.”

“You have been trespassing through private records.”

“I was invited.”

“After you forced your way onto the island.”

“Your secretary sent the letter.”

“I have no secretary.”

Orr glanced at me. “Then someone used your name.”

Kreel dabbed his mouth with a linen cloth. “Mr. Orr is conducting a personal inquiry and has mistaken coincidence for pattern. Construction is dangerous. Men fall. Boats overturn. People leave.”

“People leave,” Orr repeated. “Yet their wages continue to be drawn. Their names remain on payrolls. Their families are told different stories.”

“That is an allegation.”

“It is a discrepancy.”

“Every old account contains discrepancies.”

“Especially when the accounts have been altered.”

Celia leaned forward. “What accounts?”

“Original estate records,” Orr said. “Invoices, labor registers, payments to subcontractors. Several pages are missing from the copies held in the county archive. The missing pages concern the first foundation and the retaining wall.”

Vale’s spoon clicked against the bowl.

I watched him rather than Orr. His reaction was not surprise. It was recognition, followed immediately by control.

“What did you find?” I asked.

Orr’s fingers tightened around his napkin. “A reference to an emergency excavation. Three days of unrecorded labor. Timber purchased after the scaffold accident. Lime and stone delivered to the lower grounds at night.”

Kreel said, “That could describe any number of repairs.”

“Not if the house had not yet been occupied and the foundation had already been sealed.”

The room seemed to contract.

The pale lines in the floor, which I had taken for decorative inlay, ran beneath the table and disappeared under the walls. They looked suddenly like the outline of a diagram. A map of something hidden below us.

Vale lifted his head. “You are finished.”

Orr did not seem to hear him. “There are also references to a draftsman who disappeared during the same period. Gabriel Rusk.”

My hand closed around my fork.

Jonah had said his father had not abandoned them. He had said it once, during an interview I had conducted in a room with mirrored glass and a recorder between us. I had marked the statement as irrelevant. At the time, Gabriel Rusk had been a dead end: a vanished worker from decades earlier, a family grief Jonah used to explain why he had been searching county records.

I had believed the room more than I had believed the man.

“What happened to Gabriel?” I asked.

Agnes, behind me, made a small sound.

Vale stood.

He did not rise quickly. He unfolded himself with the effort of an old man, one hand gripping the silver head of his cane. But when he spoke, the weakness had gone from his voice.

“I said you were finished.”

Orr met his stare. “Then tell us where he is.”

The wind hit again. Rain raced sideways over the glass, blurring the sea and the reflection of everyone at the table. For an instant the reflected room seemed to contain another person behind Vale, a narrow figure standing in the dark.

I turned.

There was no one there.

Vale struck the floor with his cane.

The chandelier trembled overhead. “You come into my house with stolen fragments and accuse me of murder at my own table?”

“I asked where a man went.”

“You asked nothing. You arrived with a conclusion.”

“Because the records lead here.”

“The records lead wherever an amateur wants them to lead.”

Orr’s expression changed—not to fear, but to anger. “My grandmother kept letters from Livia Vale.”

The name landed harder than Gabriel’s.

Celia went still. Adrian looked down. Kreel’s face became unreadable.

Vale stared at Orr.

“Your grandmother,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Who was she?”

“Marian Orr.”

Vale’s mouth tightened. “Livia’s cousin.”

“Her sister.”

“Half-sister.”

“And she received letters from Livia after Gabriel disappeared.”

A glass cracked.

No one had touched it. The stem of Celia’s wineglass split beneath her fingers, and red wine ran across the white cloth like a wound. Agnes moved at once with a towel.

Vale had not looked at the glass. He was looking at Orr.

“What did the letters say?”

Orr’s hand went toward his satchel beneath the table.

Kreel spoke for the first time with an edge in his voice. “If you have documents, Mr. Orr, you should show them to the proper authorities rather than stage a family interrogation.”

“Which authorities?” Orr asked. “The ones who accepted the official accounts?”

Kreel’s gaze shifted to me. “Ms. Venn is here, is she not?”

“Former detective,” I said.

“Still an investigator, by reputation.”

“Not yours.”

His smile was faint. “No. I imagine I am not anyone’s favorite witness.”

“You reviewed the county plans in the Wren case,” I said.

The table quieted again.

Kreel did not look surprised. “I reviewed a number of plans.”

“One cross-section was initialed by you.”

“Many were.”

“It was marked NO CONCEALED ACCESS.”

“Was it inaccurate?”

“That depends on whether there was concealed access.”

“Then perhaps you should have established that before giving evidence.”

There was no defensiveness in the answer. Only a smooth reversal, so clean it might have been rehearsed.

I felt the old case stir inside me: the records room, Jonah’s hammer, the narrow window, the plans that made a route impossible. The certainty I had built from measurements and signatures. The delivery van footage I had discovered afterward, too unclear to prove anything, and my decision to leave it in a private folder because the defense could have found it.

Kreel watched my face.

He knew I was remembering.

A bell rang in the hall.

This one was clear: a single bright note.

Agnes looked toward the door.

Vale said, “The ferry.”

“No,” I said. “A ferry bell would be outside.”

Another note sounded, lower and farther away.

Adrian pushed his chair back. “Could someone tell us what is happening?”

Vale turned to Agnes. “Have you heard from the harbor?”

“Not since Mr. Sayer came up from the road.”

“Ask him to call again.”

“The telephone is dead.”

Kreel glanced toward the wall. “The line failed in the storm.”

“Then use the radio,” Vale said.

“The radio room is flooded.”

Celia stared at him. “You said the ferry was suspended.”

“I said it might be.”

“You knew before Mara arrived.”

“I knew the weather was worsening.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Vale’s eyes moved around the table. The anger had drained from him, leaving something more dangerous: calculation.

“No crossing will leave tonight,” he said. “The harbor master confirmed it before dinner. The lower road is under water, and the upper road is blocked by a fallen tree. We are here until morning.”

Adrian swore softly.

Orr’s hand remained inside his satchel.

Kreel resumed eating, as if isolation were merely another course.

I looked at the glass walls. Beyond them, the storm erased the island one section at a time. The house had become its own jurisdiction, with its own clocks, doors, and rules of movement. No one could leave. No one could summon help. Every person at the table had a motive to lie, and someone had already placed warnings where they would be found.

Vale sat down again.

“Dessert will be served in the blue room,” he said.

“No,” Celia said. “You don’t get to dismiss this.”

“I am not dismissing it.”

“You’ve been doing nothing else.”

He turned toward her. “You want to know why I have not sold the island?”

“I want to know whether you intend to.”

“I have not signed the agreement.”

“Because you’re reconsidering?”

“Because I have discovered that the land is not mine to sell.”

The words stopped her.

Vale looked at me. “There are papers I found recently. They concern the original construction, certain payments, and alterations made to this house and to another building on the mainland.”

“The county building?” I asked.

His gaze did not waver. “Among other places.”

Kreel’s knife paused against his plate.

Vale saw it. So did I.

“The papers may explain why certain people disappeared,” he continued. “They may also explain how a man was convicted for entering a room he could not have entered.”

Jonah’s name was not spoken, but it stood between us.

“Where are the papers?” I asked.

“Safe.”

“Here?”

“For the moment.”

“Who else knows about them?”

“That is what I am trying to determine.”

“You invited a historian who has been asking about the dead, a partner connected to the old plans, two children with financial motives, and a housekeeper who knows the construction history. If you wanted secrecy, you chose badly.”

A shadow of a smile touched his mouth. “I wanted witnesses.”

“To what?”

“Perhaps to the truth. Perhaps to the manner in which it is prevented.”

The phrase chilled me more than the storm.

Agnes approached to clear the soup bowls. As she leaned over my shoulder, she whispered, “Do not go where he tells you without asking why.”

I turned, but she had already moved away.

Vale rose again, this time with less effort.

“Mara,” he said, “when dinner is concluded, meet me in the observatory.”

Celia’s head snapped around. “Why there?”

“Because the observatory is private.”

“Nothing in this house is private.”

“Then you should appreciate the challenge.”

Kreel looked at him for a long moment. “The observatory is unsafe in this weather.”

“So is the dining room, apparently.”

A sharp boom sounded from somewhere below. The tableware jumped. Overhead, the chandelier swung, scattering moving shadows over the glass.

Vale did not flinch.

“Bring the Wren file,” he told me. “And come alone.”

The storm pressed its white face against the windows.

I looked at the empty chair, the darkening sea, and the people who had all just been given a reason to wonder what Vale intended to show me. Then I looked at Kreel.

He was smiling, but only with his mouth.

“Of course,” I said.

chapters.name: The Names in the Walls
chapters.content:
Agnes found me beneath the portrait of a woman whose face had been painted out.

I had left the dining room with Vale’s words still pressing between my shoulder blades—*the observatory, alone, bring the Wren file*—and had gone only as far as the western corridor before stopping. Rain struck the glass beyond the passage in silver handfuls. Somewhere inside the walls, a clock began to count and then lost interest after four chimes.

Agnes stood at the end of the corridor carrying a tray with two untouched cups of tea.

“You should not go to him yet,” she said.

“I wasn’t aware I’d announced my intentions.”

“You have the look.”

“I have several looks. Most of them are unflattering.”

She glanced toward the dining room. Through the open doorway I could see Celia arguing with Adrian in low, vicious voices. Kreel had remained at the table, one hand resting beside his wineglass, listening without appearing to listen. Orr was staring at the rain and touching the flap of his canvas satchel.

Agnes lowered her voice. “Come with me.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere the walls do not repeat us.”

That was not a reassuring invitation. In Blackwater House, walls seemed to have more loyalties than people did.

Still, I followed her.

She led me down a narrow service passage behind the kitchen, past shelves of preserves and a dumbwaiter with its rope cut short. The passage ended at a door painted the same black as the stone. Agnes pressed her palm against a brass plate, and a section of wall released with a soft internal click.

Beyond it was a cramped room with no furniture except a wooden stool and a bank of old speaking tubes. Their brass mouths protruded from the wall at different heights. One had been sealed with wax. Another whispered faintly whenever the wind struck the house.

Agnes shut the panel behind us.

“I knew Gabriel Rusk,” she said.

The name entered the room like a person.

I looked at her. “You knew him well?”

“Well enough.”

“Did he work here?”

“He worked everywhere here. When Mr. Vale began building Blackwater, Gabriel was the draftsman. He drew the plans, measured the foundations, argued with the engineers, and corrected mistakes before they became expensive.” Her hands trembled slightly as she set the tray on the stool. “He could look at a line and know if it was lying.”

“That sounds like a useful talent.”

“It was not always appreciated.”

The house groaned around us. A deep, shifting sound traveled through the floor and up the speaking tubes. Agnes waited until it passed.

“What happened to him?” I asked.

“An accident.”

“Which accident?”

“The scaffold collapse.”

I knew the answer before she said it, though I did not know why.

“Gabriel died during construction?”

“That was the account.”

“Was it true?”

Agnes’s mouth tightened. “There was a scaffold accident. A section of it gave way near the first foundation. Men were working below. Gabriel was there.”

“His body was found?”

She looked at the sealed speaking tube.

“No.”

The room seemed to contract around us.

“Then how was he presumed dead?”

“His coat was found. His drafting case was found. One boot.” She said this without emphasis, as if the absence of a man could be itemized with his belongings. “The lower excavation flooded soon afterward. Mr. Vale said the body must have been carried beneath the rubble. They brought in timber, lime, and stone. The wall was finished.”

“Without recovering him?”

“Storm was coming. The contractors said the ground was unsafe. They had families. Wages. Orders.”

“Whose orders?”

Agnes looked at me then. Her eyes were pale and tired, but fear moved behind them with the practiced speed of a fish beneath dark water.

“Mr. Vale’s,” she said.

“And Kreel’s?”

She did not answer.

I thought of Simon Kreel at the dinner table, speaking of ordinary errors in old accounts. *Three days of unrecorded labor. Timber after a scaffold accident. Lime and stone delivered at night.* He had made history sound like a housekeeper’s untidy cupboard.

“Gabriel Rusk,” I said slowly. “He had a family?”

“A wife. A son.”

“What son?”

Agnes turned away.

I had carried the name for six years. I had spoken it in court, written it into reports, watched a clerk print it on the spine of a file.

“Jonah,” I said.

The word was barely louder than the rain.

Agnes closed her eyes.

“Jonah Rusk was Gabriel’s son.”

The room’s narrowness became physical. I felt the old case open inside me, not as memory but as a wound someone had put a hand into.

Daniel Wren’s body in the county records room. The surveyor’s hammer beside him. Jonah standing in the corridor with rain on his shoulders, saying his father had not abandoned the family. I had thought it was grief looking for a shape. A son protecting a dead man’s reputation. A private obsession with the records Gabriel had left behind.

I had never asked what Gabriel Rusk might have been trying to find.

“What did Jonah know?” I asked.

“He knew his father had not run away.”

“That is not what the official account said.”

“Official accounts are often made by people who were not there.”

“Did you tell him what happened?”

“I was a maid. He was a child when Gabriel vanished. By the time he was old enough to ask, the family had gone from the island. His mother did not want him digging into it.”

“Why not?”

Agnes folded her hands together. The skin over her knuckles was thin and spotted.

“Because she was afraid.”

“Of Vale?”

“Of what happened to people who insisted on being remembered.”

The old phrase from Vale’s warning surfaced in my mind: *made to disappear as the others did.*

I thought of the photograph beside the first foundation, the blurred man near the unfinished wall. I thought of the red mark on the observatory glass. I thought of Jonah’s hammer, supposedly stolen while he searched the records concerning his father.

“Was Gabriel killed?” I asked.

Agnes’s face changed. Not much. A tightening at the corners of her eyes, a slight withdrawal of her chin. But I had spent eighteen years watching people decide whether to lie.

“You should ask Mr. Vale,” she said.

“He has asked me to meet him alone in a room full of concealed machinery during a storm.”

“That is why I am telling you not to go without asking why.”

“You already told me that.”

“I meant it.”

“Then tell me what I should ask.”

She stared at the brass speaking tubes. “Ask who was below the house when Gabriel disappeared.”

“Who?”

“Not who was working. Who was *below*.”

A metallic knock traveled through the wall behind us.

Agnes flinched.

I heard it too: three taps, deliberate and evenly spaced.

“Is there someone on the other side?” I asked.

“No.”

The tapping came again.

Agnes hurried to the sealed tube and pressed both hands over its mouth. The wax trembled.

“Do these still work?”

“Some do.”

“Who can speak through them?”

“Anyone who knows the routes.”

“Does Kreel know the routes?”

She gave me a look that was almost pity. “Mr. Kreel knows the house better than Mr. Vale.”

The tapping stopped.

For a moment, neither of us moved.

Then I said, “What happened to Livia?”

Agnes’s hands fell from the tube.

“Mrs. Vale?”

“You said Gabriel’s wife was afraid. Livia was Vale’s wife. Did she know what happened to Gabriel?”

“She knew enough.”

“Enough to do what?”

“Enough to leave.”

“Leave Blackwater?”

Agnes’s expression became distant, and I understood that she was looking not at me but through the years. “Mrs. Livia was never comfortable here. She said the house had too many ways to put a person where nobody could find them. Mr. Vale thought she was being dramatic. He called it imagination.”

“Yet she vanished.”

“Twenty-nine years ago.”

“The official story was a boating accident?”

“So they said.”

“Her body was never recovered?”

“No.”

“Boat?”

“Found against the rocks below the east cliff. One oar missing. Her shawl caught on the railing.”

“Was there blood?”

Agnes looked at me sharply. “Why?”

“Because objects can be placed. Bodies can be moved. Boats can be made to tell stories.”

She lowered herself onto the stool. The tea on the tray trembled in its cups.

“Mrs. Livia had written letters,” she said. “To her sister. She said Gabriel had discovered payments that did not make sense. Men being paid after they disappeared. Materials sent to places no one could identify. She said he had found alterations in the plans—passages, chambers, foundations—that were not recorded in the final drawings.”

I thought of the cross-section in the Wren file.

**NO CONCEALED ACCESS. S.K.**

“Did she name Kreel?”

Agnes’s gaze moved to the door.

“Mrs. Livia named everyone in private.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” she whispered. “It is not.”

A faint sound came from the corridor. Footsteps, perhaps, or water moving in the pipes.

I stood and put my good hand on the door latch. “We need to leave.”

Agnes caught my sleeve.

“Did you see someone?” I asked.

“I saw Mr. Vale after Gabriel disappeared.”

“What do you mean?”

“He was covered in mud.”

“Vale?”

“He came into the kitchen before dawn. His hands were bleeding. Not badly. Scratches, mostly. He asked for brandy and told me there had been an accident near the foundation. He said Gabriel was dead.”

“Did he say he had seen the body?”

“No.”

“Did he say who else was there?”

Her fingers tightened around my sleeve.

“Mrs. Livia,” she said.

The door latch clicked.

Agnes released me so suddenly that I stumbled against the speaking tubes. One of them gave a hollow cough.

I pulled the door open.

The service passage was empty.

At the far end, a rectangle of warmer light lay across the floor from the kitchen. No one stood in it. I stepped out and scanned the walls, the ceiling, the joints between the black stone panels. Blackwater’s corridors made absence feel deliberate.

Agnes came behind me and shut the hidden door.

“You saw nothing,” she said.

“I saw an empty passage.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.”

She took the tray again, though her hands were steadier now. “You must not tell Mr. Vale I spoke to you.”

“Why?”

“Because he will ask what I said.”

“And you don’t want to lie to him?”

“I have lied to him for forty years.”

That stopped me.

“To protect whom?”

“Sometimes him. Sometimes myself. Sometimes the dead.”

She turned toward the kitchen.

“Agnes.”

She paused.

“Did Gabriel die beneath this house?”

For several seconds the only answer was the rain battering the glass roof above us.

Then she said, “Ask what was buried.”

It was the same sentence as Vale’s message, but in her voice it became an instruction rather than a warning.

She walked away before I could ask anything else.

I remained in the passage, listening to her steps diminish. The thought of the observatory waited at the end of the house like a second interrogation. Vale wanted me alone. Kreel wanted me uncertain. Agnes wanted me afraid enough to ask the right question.

I went back to the dining room.

Celia was standing by the window with her arms folded. Adrian had poured himself another drink, though his hand shook too badly to keep the glass from spilling. Orr looked up at me, and for an instant I wondered whether he had been listening through one of the walls.

Kreel smiled.

It was a small, courteous expression. The kind used by men who have already heard the answer to a question they have not asked.

“Did you find the observatory?” he said.

“Not yet.”

“It is difficult to navigate when one is unfamiliar with the house.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“Vale should have sent someone with you.”

“He specifically asked me to go alone.”

Kreel’s smile did not change. “Elias has always enjoyed theater.”

“Do you know why he wants the Wren file?”

“Because he thinks his house is responsible for everything unpleasant that has happened in his life.”

“Is it?”

The question seemed to amuse him.

“Architecture is blamed for many things. Bad marriages. Failed businesses. Missing persons. Murder.” He lifted his glass. “It is rarely responsible.”

Orr stood. “What did Agnes tell you?”

“Nothing.”

“Agnes tells everyone nothing.”

“Then we have something in common.”

Thunder rolled above us. The lights flickered once, twice. Every face in the room sharpened and blurred with the pulses.

Vale appeared in the doorway.

He had changed nothing about his clothing, but the storm had altered him. His hair was damp, and one sleeve was darkened from wrist to elbow. He looked less like a host than a man who had just returned from somewhere he had not intended anyone to see.

“Mara,” he said. “You are late.”

“Your house has a complicated route to the observatory.”

“Most useful things do.”

Kreel rose. “Elias, perhaps you should postpone this.”

Vale’s gaze moved to him. “Perhaps you should stop offering advice.”

For the first time, Kreel’s composure thinned.

Vale looked back at me. “Come.”

I did not move. “Did your wife die in a boating accident?”

The room went still.

Adrian’s glass stopped halfway to his mouth. Celia turned from the window. Orr’s hand went to his satchel.

Vale’s face emptied itself.

“Who told you that?”

“Is it true?”

“You have been speaking with Agnes.”

“I asked whether it was true.”

He looked toward the ceiling, as though waiting for the house to answer on his behalf. Somewhere above us, machinery clicked. The sound seemed to come from inside the walls and from beneath the floor at once.

“Livia disappeared,” he said. “The boat was found. She was not.”

“Did you believe she was dead?”

“I believed she had gone beyond my ability to find her.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.” His voice cracked on the word. “It is not.”

Celia stared at him. “You said she fell.”

“I said what the police required.”

“You said what was convenient.”

Vale gripped the doorframe. For a moment I thought he might collapse, but the weakness passed and left something harder behind.

“Mrs. Vale knew too much,” he said. “That was her danger.”

“What did she know?”

His eyes met mine.

“About the first foundation.”

The lights went out.

Not dimmed. Not flickered. Every bulb in the dining room, the corridor, and the distant hall vanished in the same instant.

Blackwater became a single sound: rain, wind, the groan of stressed metal, and the sudden startled breathing of the living.

Someone knocked over a chair.

Adrian swore. Celia cried out—not in fear, but anger—and a door slammed somewhere beyond the dining room.

In the darkness, Vale said my name.

Then another voice answered from inside the walls.

chapters.name: The Blackout
chapters.content:
The voice answered from inside the walls.

“Here.”

It was not loud. That made it worse. A whisper might belong to the house; a human voice had to belong to someone.

I stood with one hand on the back of my chair, the dining room black around me. Rain hammered the glass roof with such force that the whole ceiling seemed to shiver. Somewhere beyond it, thunder rolled over the island and sank into the stone foundations.

Nobody moved.

Then Adrian knocked against the table.

“Damn it.”

A chair leg scraped. Someone inhaled sharply. The smell of overturned wine rose from the darkness.

“Who said that?” Celia demanded.

No answer came.

Vale called again, seemingly closer this time. “Mara.”

I turned toward him. In the dark, direction was a suggestion. The room had too many hard surfaces, too many angled walls and concealed apertures. A voice could enter through a speaking tube and arrive from anywhere. The sound might have come from Vale himself, from the corridor, or from a mouth pressed against a grille inside the wall.

“Don’t move,” I said.

“I’m not moving,” Vale replied.

Something struck the floor near my shoes. A glass rolled in a slow circle until it touched my chair.

Celia made a small sound of disgust or fear. “What was that?”

“Stay where you are.”

A door slammed somewhere beyond the room.

The sound broke the spell. Chairs scraped back. Celia called her father’s name. Agnes asked for a lamp. Adrian swore, and someone struck the table hard enough to make the cutlery jump.

I reached into my coat for the flashlight I carried, but found the pocket empty.

I had left it in the hall.

For one second, I considered staying where I was. The person who had spoken from the walls might be in the room with us. The person who had moved the glass might be reaching for a weapon. But the crash that followed came from the library, and Lucan Orr had gone there before the blackout to examine the old plans.

I crossed the room with one hand on the table. Bodies shifted around me. Someone’s shoulder struck mine.

“Careful,” Kreel said.

“Where is Vale?”

“He was beside the fireplace.”

“He was beside you,” Celia said.

“I know where I was.”

At the doorway I pressed my palm to the wall. Cold stone, damp at the seam. If the voice had come through a tube, I might feel a vibration. There was nothing. Only the faint tremor of the storm moving through the masonry.

“Mara.”

The voice came from the left.

I turned. “Vale?”

No answer.

A crash sounded from the library.

“Orr,” Agnes said.

I ran.

The hall twisted after six steps, or seemed to. My shoulder struck a projecting corner. In the darkness, the corridor had become a throat, narrowing and widening without warning. I kept moving, using the wall to stay oriented. Another noise came ahead: a fall, then breaking glass.

The library door stood open. I entered with my hands raised, expecting an attacker at arm’s length.

Nothing touched me.

The air smelled of dust, leather, and metal. Beside the display case, a man groaned.

“Orr?”

“Here.”

I dropped to one knee and found his sleeve. He seized my wrist with surprising strength.

“Don’t stand there.”

“Are you hurt?”

“My head.”

“Can you move your legs?”

“Yes.”

“Then crawl toward my voice.”

He obeyed, dragging himself across the carpet. I kept one hand on his shoulder and the other extended before me. A chair had fallen nearby. The room seemed full of shapes that might become people.

“What happened?” I asked.

“The case. I was looking at the plans. Something came from behind me.”

“Something?”

“A blow. A hand, perhaps. I don’t know.”

“Did you see who?”

“No. I heard the shelves move.”

Behind us, footsteps approached. A narrow beam of light entered the room. Kreel stood in the doorway with a brass oil lamp.

“Is he alive?” he asked.

“Barely.”

“I’ll fetch Agnes.”

“She’s coming.”

The lamp revealed Orr sprawled beside the case, blood in his hair, a bronze bust on its side. The glass was fractured and the case door open. The bust was heavy enough to stun a man. Its polished face stared upward with blind dignity.

“What were you examining?” I asked.

Orr reached toward the case. “The foundation records. The original surveys.”

“Which one?”

“The cross-section. The one marked NO CONCEALED ACCESS.”

I felt through the folders and broken glass. The document was gone.

Kreel crouched beside Orr. “Can you stand?”

“I can stand,” Orr said, though he made no attempt.

“Don’t touch anything,” I told Kreel.

“I was helping.”

“Help by standing still.”

Celia appeared carrying a candle, followed by Adrian and Agnes. The candle flame shook in Celia’s hand, throwing her face into alternating planes of light and shadow.

“Where is my father?” she asked.

“Wasn’t he with you?”

“He was in the dining room.”

“He left before the crash,” Kreel said.

Celia turned on him. “You were not there.”

“I came when I heard Orr.”

“I was in the west passage,” Kreel said.

“Repairing the generator,” I replied.

“Yes.”

“Then why are you carrying a lamp?”

“Because the generator has not restarted.”

The flame guttered. For an instant I saw a thin vertical seam behind the display case, a door concealed in the paneling. Then the light steadied, and it vanished into the grain of the shelves.

Agnes brought cloth. Celia fetched the first-aid box. Adrian went to search the hall.

The generator coughed in the distance. The house trembled, as if something enormous had turned in its sleep. The lights returned a moment later, yellow and uneven. Several bulbs flickered, then steadied. The electric glow made the blood on Orr’s face seem black.

The display case held an empty rectangle where the document had been. Dust outlined the missing folder. A sliver of paper remained caught beneath the brass lip.

I bent over it without touching the case.

The document had been removed cleanly. The attacker had not taken it in confusion. They had known exactly which sheet they wanted.

Orr sat against the desk while Agnes bound his head.

“That is the service corridor,” Kreel said, looking at the bookcase.

“You know that now?”

“I knew it before.”

“Open it.”

He reached toward the shelf.

“Use your left hand,” I said.

He stopped. “Why?”

“Your right hand is clean. Your left sleeve is wet.”

He looked down. The cuff of his left sleeve was dark with rain or water. It might have come from the generator room. It might have come from somewhere else.

“Your suspicion is theatrical,” he said.

“It has had a good evening.”

Celia pressed the bandage to Orr’s scalp. “He needs a doctor.”

“There is no doctor on the island,” Agnes said. “Not until morning.”

“Then he needs to remain conscious.”

“I am conscious,” Orr muttered.

“Good. Stay that way.”

I looked at the bookcase. Its open inch had become an accusation. In that darkness anyone might have looked tall. The attacker had not come merely to hurt Orr. They had taken the cross-section.

“Who knew he was examining it?” I asked.

No one answered.

Vale had known. Orr had known. Kreel might have known if he had been watching. Agnes had seen Orr in the library. Celia had asked what he was reading at dinner. I had told Vale that the old plans mattered to me.

“Search the house,” I said.

Celia stared at me. “Now?”

“We find Vale first. Then the document.”

“We can’t search every room in this place.”

“Then we search the rooms people have reason to enter.”

Kreel straightened. “Everyone stays together.”

“Good. Celia, stay with Orr and Agnes. Adrian, come with me.”

Adrian looked from me to the blood on Orr’s face. “Why me?”

“Because you were the last person to claim you were looking for your father.”

“And you trust me?”

“I don’t.”

His jaw tightened, but he followed.

We started in the dining room. Vale’s chair stood pulled back from the table. His glass remained untouched. A folded napkin had fallen to the floor, and one of the candles had burned nearly to its base. Near the fireplace, a dark smear crossed the stone.

I crouched beside it.

Mud, not wine. A narrow mark led toward the western doorway and ended at the threshold. The print beside it was incomplete, as though someone had stepped backward or dragged a wet sole across the floor.

“Was that there before?” I asked.

Celia called from the library, “I don’t know.”

Adrian bent over it. “Could be from Vale’s shoe.”

“Could be.”

“His sleeve was wet,” Adrian said. “You noticed that.”

“Before the blackout.”

“Then perhaps he went outside.”

“In that storm?”

“Perhaps he had a reason.”

Everyone in the house had a reason. That was the trouble. A reason was not a route, and a route was not proof.

We checked the study. It was empty. Desk drawers stood open, and envelopes lay scattered across the floor. One had been torn in half. I picked up the pieces.

Three words, in Vale’s hand:

NOT YET. WAIT.

No recipient.

Adrian watched me read. “He wrote a lot of things to himself.”

“Did he?”

“He was strange.”

“Where were you when the lights failed?”

“In the hall outside the dining room.”

“Did you hear the voice?”

He hesitated. “Yes.”

“What did it say?”

“Here.”

“Whose voice was it?”

“I don’t know.”

“You didn’t recognize it?”

He looked toward the door. “It sounded like my father.”

“Why didn’t you say that?”

“Because I thought it was him.”

“And now?”

“Now he’s missing.”

His answer was too quick, but fear had a way of making rehearsed statements resemble honesty. I searched his face. Adrian looked frightened, not just of what had happened but of what his father’s absence might mean for him.

We went toward the west corridor. Kreel waited there with his lamp, though the electric lights had returned.

“You cannot search the generator room without me,” he said.

“Why not?”

“The machinery is dangerous.”

“So is the rest of this house.”

He led us through a narrow passage where pipes and brass inspection plates interrupted the stone. The generator room smelled of oil and hot dust. A belt had come loose from its wheel, and the fuel coupling sat on a shelf.

“This was deliberately loosened,” I said.

“You are not qualified to diagnose machinery.”

“I’m qualified to recognize something unscrewed by hand.”

“The vibration shook it free.”

“Then why is the coupling on the shelf?”

He had no answer.

Adrian gave a nervous laugh. “Maybe the house did it.”

Kreel looked at him. “Do not be clever.”

At the far end, a maintenance hatch stood open. Beyond it came the smell of rain.

“Where does that go?” I asked.

“Drainage access.”

“Large enough for a person?”

“Barely.”

“Have you used it tonight?”

“No.”

“Can you prove that?”

He gave me a flat smile. “You are welcome to crawl through.”

I took the lamp from him and knelt. A low passage ran behind the walls, slick with condensation, bending out of sight. Fresh mud marked the floor. Near the hatch, one of the marks contained a distinct heel pattern. I could not tell whether it was a boot or a shoe.

It ended at a metal grille over the cliffside drainage channel, where black water surged through the opening. The tide and rain had turned it into a roaring throat.

No Vale. No document.

Only another route by which the house could pretend to have swallowed someone.

We returned to the central hall. Orr sat beneath the staircase, Agnes pressing the bandage to his head. Celia stood beside him with her arms folded tightly across her chest. She watched Kreel as if she had just discovered a weapon in his hand.

“Nothing,” I said.

Kreel looked toward the stairs. “The storm has taken him.”

“People do not vanish because weather is dramatic.”

“On this island, they do.”

His words echoed Agnes’s warning. People who insisted on being remembered could disappear.

I looked around the hall: suspended stairs, black-glass panels, doors set at deceptive angles. The blackout had lasted perhaps four minutes. In that time someone had attacked Orr, removed a document, interfered with the generator, and possibly lured Vale away—or made it appear that he had gone.

The order mattered.

A crime scene was not only where violence occurred. It was where someone wanted the violence understood.

Orr’s wound made him a witness. The missing cross-section could make him a suspect, or give someone a reason to suggest one. The failed generator offered an alibi to whoever claimed to be repairing it. Vale’s disappearance gave us a more urgent mystery than the broken case.

And the voice from the wall had made certain we knew the house was involved.

“Everyone stays in the central hall,” I said. “No one touches the display case, the generator, or any unchecked door.”

Celia’s face was pale. “You think my father is dead.”

“I think he is missing.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer I can prove.”

“You were brought here to protect him,” Kreel said.

“I was brought here because he thought the truth had been hidden in the walls.”

“And now you believe every wall is a suspect.”

“Walls don’t remove documents.”

“People do. People with motives.”

“Then you should be pleased. We have several.”

His gaze settled on me. “You have done this before.”

The words were mild. The effect was not. For a moment I saw the county records room again: the locked door, the hammer, Jonah Rusk’s exhausted face as I explained how the evidence could only mean one thing.

Only one thing.

I had built a life out of those words and abandoned the police when I learned how easily they became a lie. Now someone had taken a page from an old case and struck a witness in the dark. It was not coincidence. It was a message, whether the message was meant for me or for everyone.

From somewhere above us came a soft metallic click.

A second followed, then a slow dragging sound within the walls, moving toward the observatory.

Everyone heard it. Orr lifted his head. Agnes went still. Adrian whispered his father’s name.

Vale’s voice did not call again.

I took the lamp from Kreel’s hand.

“Now,” I said, “we search the upper floor.”

chapters.name: The Sealed Observatory
chapters.content:
The sound moved above us.

Three metallic clicks, then a dragging noise that seemed to travel through the walls rather than along them. Blackwater carried sound badly; a whisper could arrive from a ceiling, a footstep from behind a door. But this vibration came through the soles of my shoes and climbed the bones of my legs.

Everyone in the central hall heard it.

Adrian gripped the back of a chair. Celia turned toward the suspended staircase. Agnes folded her arms tightly across her chest, as though holding herself together. Kreel held the brass oil lamp at shoulder height, its flame throwing a restless oval over the black stone walls.

Another click sounded, sharper than the first.

“The observatory,” Kreel said.

He said it too quickly.

I took the lamp from him. His fingers remained around the handle for half a second before he released it.

“Stay here,” I said.

Celia gave a short, bitter laugh. “You think the person who took my father will wait politely while you investigate?”

“I think I have one lamp, and I’m not taking six people into a house full of unverified doors.”

“My father may be dying.”

“My father may be anywhere,” Adrian said. “He could be hiding from us. He could have started this himself.”

Celia turned on him. “You hope he has.”

Adrian’s face tightened. “And you hope he’s dead, because then the house goes to you.”

“Enough,” I said.

The word struck the hall and seemed to return from somewhere behind us.

I looked from one face to the next. Fear had made them honest in small, unhelpful ways. Adrian’s eyes were fixed on the stairs, but his shoulders angled toward the study wing. Celia had one hand pressed against the side of her coat, where the folded copy of something—perhaps a letter, perhaps one of the papers she had stolen from Vale—made a square beneath the fabric. Agnes watched the walls. Kreel watched me.

“You all remain in this hall,” I said. “No one follows unless I call for help.”

Kreel’s mouth moved faintly. “You can’t order us around.”

“I can order you not to contaminate a scene.”

“Nothing’s happened yet.”

I held his gaze. “That’s what I’m trying to preserve.”

Adrian straightened. “I’m coming.”

“No.”

“You need someone to see what you can’t.”

“I need someone not to walk behind me.”

His expression hardened into the resentment he wore more naturally than fear. “You can’t make me stay.”

“No,” I said. “But if you enter a room after me, I’ll treat you as a potential suspect who ignored a direct warning. Decide whether that helps you.”

He looked toward Celia for support. She gave him none.

Agnes touched Celia’s sleeve. “Let her go. If there is anything left to find, she must find it before the house changes it.”

Celia stared at the walls. “The house doesn’t change things.”

“No,” Agnes said. “People do.”

I carried the lamp to the staircase.

The suspended steps rose from the hall without visible support, each dark slab held out from the wall by a narrow steel spine. Vale had called the staircase an exercise in optical uncertainty. In the storm-dark it seemed to shift as I climbed, some steps receding, others thrusting forward. The lamp made the lower stairs bright and the upper ones indistinct, so that I could never see more than five at a time.

Halfway up, I heard a faint tremor beneath my palm where it rested on the rail.

The mechanism was still moving.

At the upper landing, a narrow corridor ran east through panels of smoked glass. Water ticked somewhere inside the structure. The metallic scraping had stopped.

At the end stood the observatory door.

It was made of blackened steel set into a stone frame, with a heavy handle and a round brass plate at eye level. I tried the handle. It did not turn.

“Celia,” I called. “Does anyone have the observatory key?”

“My father does,” she answered from the stairwell. “Kreel may have one.”

“No,” Kreel called.

“Only him?”

“Vale kept the observatory locked.”

“Did he carry the key?”

A pause.

“Always,” Kreel said.

I examined the door. There was no keyhole on the corridor side, only the compass-shaped brass plate. Four points radiated from a small central circle. The design had appeared on Vale’s papers, on the carved stone Agnes had shown me, and on the old instrument in the observatory. A decorative emblem, I had assumed. Blackwater had taught me to distrust decoration.

I pressed the plate, then ran my fingers along the frame. No catch or auxiliary latch revealed itself. The steel was cold enough to numb my fingertips.

“Vale?” I called.

For several seconds there was no answer. The storm filled the silence: rain striking glass, wind dragging itself along the roof, the distant concussion of surf against the cliff.

Then something struck the floor inside.

Celia made a small, strangled sound.

“Is he there?” she asked.

I crouched and looked through the narrow gap beneath the door. A lightning flash illuminated the chamber beyond: glass walls, an overturned chair, and a figure lying on its side several feet from the entrance.

The light vanished.

“Is he alive?” Celia asked.

I looked again during the next flash. The figure had not moved.

“I don’t know yet.”

Kreel came up the stairs carrying a long iron bar. I had not heard him leave the hall.

“Where did you find that?” I asked.

“Maintenance cupboard.”

He offered it to me. I took it, careful not to touch the end more than necessary.

“Stay where I can see you.”

“I’m not the one with the weapon.”

“That isn’t why.”

His expression did not change, but his eyes went to the brass plate. He recognized something about the door—or was pretending to.

I wedged the bar between the door and frame near the latch. The steel had been built to withstand the pressure of the sea wind. My first attempt failed. The second bent the end of the bar.

“Try the upper hinge,” Kreel said. “The lower one is reinforced.”

I looked at him.

“How do you know that?”

“I restored the door.”

“Three decades ago?”

“Some things don’t change.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the one you have.”

I shifted the bar to the upper hinge. The lamp flame guttered as a blast of wind struck the corridor. Behind me Celia climbed another step, and I heard Adrian tell her to stop.

On the third attempt, the metal screamed. The frame creaked, and the door moved less than an inch before striking something on the floor.

I lowered the lamp. A chair leg lay against the threshold.

“Someone put the chair there,” Celia whispered.

“Or it fell there.”

“From what?”

“From someone falling.”

I levered again. The chair scraped away with a long, deliberate sound. The door opened wide enough for me to pass sideways.

I raised the lamp and entered.

The observatory was circular in intention, though its glass walls broke the curve into sharp facets. Rain streamed down every pane. Beyond them the sea vanished and returned with each flash of lightning. The room smelled of wet metal, old dust, and something bitter that I could not identify.

Elias Vale lay beside the astronomical table.

He was on his right side, his head against the black stone. His eyes were open, reflecting the lamp in two dull points. A damp patch darkened the silver hair near his temple, but there was no obvious wound. His mouth had fallen slightly open. One cheek rested against the floor as if he had lowered himself there and forgotten to rise.

The key was in his left hand.

His fingers curled tightly around it, the brass shaft showing between the first and second fingers. Its narrow oval bow bore the same four-pointed compass design as the plate on the door.

I set the lamp on the table and did not touch him.

Body. Key. Locked door. Overturned chair. Glass walls. Storm. No visible weapon.

I repeated the list silently. The temptation was to combine those facts into a story: Vale had been lured here, followed, killed, and left behind a locked door. But a theory was often only a fact wearing a uniform. I had learned that too late in my career.

The room in the Wren case had seemed just as complete. Door locked from inside. Window too narrow. Vent opening onto dead masonry. Jonah’s hammer beside the body. I had called the arrangement a chain of facts. It had been a chain of assumptions, each link polished by my certainty.

I would not do that here.

Not yet.

I examined the nearest window latch with my eyes. It was closed and sealed inside the steel frame. The next was the same. The seams were too narrow for a hand, much less a person. There was no balcony or ledge beyond the glass. The bridge was the only visible approach.

Through the rain, I could see its iron walkway extending from the tower to the upper terrace. It was narrow and exposed. Anyone crossing would have been visible in a lightning flash, and the wind would have driven rain into their clothes. There was no wet trail across the observatory floor.

I crouched near Vale.

The dark patch by his temple was not blood. His collar and shoulder were dry. His clothes were the same as at dinner, though his left sleeve—damp earlier—now appeared dry. His right hand lay open. The left remained clenched around the key.

I placed two fingers against his neck.

Nothing.

I left them there a moment longer, pressing gently beneath the jaw. The skin was cool, though not cold. I looked at his eyes, then at his chest, though I knew there would be no movement.

He was dead.

A small sound came from the stairwell. Celia’s breath catching, perhaps, or Adrian’s. I did not look back.

“Don’t come in,” I said.

“That’s my father,” Celia replied.

“And now it’s a crime scene.”

“He may have been alive when you came through the door.”

“He wasn’t.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I checked.”

She pulled once against my hand when I caught her arm at the threshold, then stopped. Her eyes stayed on Vale’s face.

“If you touch him,” I said, “you may destroy evidence that tells us what happened.”

“My father is evidence?”

“Tonight, everything is.”

The cruelty of the answer landed. Her mouth trembled, but she did not cry. Vale’s daughter had the same talent he did for keeping grief behind the teeth.

Agnes came to stand beside her but did not enter. “God keep us,” she whispered.

“Kreel had access to everything,” she added, looking at the key. “But not Vale’s clothing, perhaps.”

Kreel remained in the corridor. “Access to the house is not the same as access to Vale’s pockets.”

“No,” I said. “It isn’t.”

I moved around the body without stepping near the center of the floor. Vale’s shoes were clean except for a thin line of gray grit along one sole. His trouser cuffs were dry. There was no sign he had crossed the exposed bridge during the storm.

The astronomical table stood beneath the glass dome, its brass rings and graduated arcs frozen in layered complexity. One ring still turned slowly. Each partial rotation ended in a faint mechanical click.

The sound from the walls.

Near the table, a small brass lever quivered and settled. I leaned closer without touching it. A narrow panel stood open beneath the meridian circle, revealing gears in shadow. A dark smear gleamed along one edge. Grease, perhaps. Or oil from the mechanism.

I did not reach inside. Whatever lay there might explain the noise—or Vale’s death—and my hand would only add another uncertainty.

“Is that blood?” Celia asked.

She had leaned forward.

“No.”

“What is it?”

“Don’t step closer.”

She stopped.

I went to the glass wall nearest the bridge. The panels were sealed by internal latches. Rain crawled along the metal frames, but the interior remained dry. I checked the lower seams for scratches, dust displacement, or a gap concealed behind the sill. Nothing. The bridge began outside the door and crossed a gap over black water. Its rails shone briefly with each lightning flash. Nothing moved across it.

“Did anyone see the bridge after the blackout?” I asked.

Adrian stood on the landing. “No.”

“Kreel?”

“I was below.”

“Agnes?”

“I stayed in the hall with Miss Celia.”

Celia said, “I heard the mechanism before the dragging sound.”

“What mechanism?”

“The bridge. Or something like it.”

“Did you see your father leave the hall?”

“No.”

“Did you see him enter the observatory?”

She looked at the body. “I saw him carrying a folder. He told me he had work to do.”

“When?”

“Before dinner. Or after. I don’t know. The clocks—”

“Approximate.”

“Half an hour before the lights went out.”

That put Vale alive in the house before the blackout, but not necessarily in the observatory afterward. The answers formed a perimeter around the room, but none of them closed it. Every person had been somewhere, and every somewhere in Blackwater was capable of lying.

I took out my notebook. Its pages were damp from the passage below. My watch had stopped during the blackout, so I recorded the time as approximate and noted the storm. I wrote down the condition of the door, the body, the key in Vale’s left hand, the sealed windows, the extended bridge, the overturned chair, the red mark, the moving mechanism, and the absence of wet tracks.

Then I wrote:

**No conclusion as to cause or time of death.**

I underlined it.

Kreel said, “You can’t leave him like that.”

“I can’t move him until the physician examines him.”

“The island physician is across the road.”

“The road is under water.”

“Then send someone.”

“No one leaves the hall alone.”

A faint smile touched his mouth. “You’re making rules for a dead man’s house.”

“I’m making rules because the dead man’s house has already lied to us twice tonight.”

The smile vanished.

I looked at Vale again.

He had summoned me with a reference to a house designed to lie. He had promised to explain what lay beneath it. Instead he had entered a room no one could enter after him and died with its key in his hand.

Or so the room wanted me to believe.

That thought was not evidence. I did not write it down.

“Everyone back downstairs,” I said. “No one touches the door, the table, the body, or the bridge. Agnes, keep Orr where he is. Adrian, stay with him. Celia—”

“I’m not going anywhere without knowing who killed my father.”

“Neither am I.”

Kreel watched me from the corridor, his face half in darkness. “You think this is murder already?”

“I think a dead man behind a locked door requires an explanation.”

“Natural causes require one too.”

“Then you’ll be pleased to wait for the physician.”

“You’re frightened of naming what you see.”

I turned toward him. “I’m frightened of naming it before I know it.”

For the first time, his composure showed a crack—not fear, exactly, but irritation at being denied the shape of the story.

The lamp flame bent toward the wall.

Somewhere inside the observatory, a mechanism clicked.

Then the door began to swing shut behind us.

chapters.name: What Everyone Heard
chapters.content:
The door swung toward us with the slow weight of a vault.

I caught it before the latch met the frame. The iron bar struck the floor, and the sound rang around the observatory. Above us, concealed machinery clicked in sequence. Something wanted the door shut.

“Don’t touch it,” Kreel said.

“I’m holding it.”

“That is what I mean.”

Celia stood behind me, one hand against the astronomical table. Agnes had backed into the curved glass wall, her face pale. Kreel was watching the mechanism, not Vale.

That was the first thing I wrote down after we forced the door wide enough to leave.

Kreel watched the mechanism.

“Can it be stopped?” I asked.

“Probably.”

“Probably isn’t useful.”

“It’s an old house. Old things move.”

“So do people.”

His eyes came to mine. “You’re suggesting I moved the door?”

“I’m suggesting nothing yet.”

It was not entirely true. But suspicion was not evidence, and I had once built a conviction out of the gap between those two things.

I kept the bar in place while Celia and Agnes passed into the corridor. Kreel followed. When I withdrew it, the door closed at once, the latch sliding home with a hard click.

Adrian, waiting below the suspended stairs, looked up.

“That was the lock,” he said.

“No. That was the door.”

“It sounded like the lock.”

“It often does.”

“Did you see him?” Celia asked.

“Your father?”

“Alive.”

The question had been waiting in her since we entered. She needed to know whether Elias Vale had crossed that threshold as a living man, or whether the house had carried his body there afterward.

“I saw him on the floor,” I said. “I didn’t see him enter.”

“Then no one did.”

“Someone did.”

Rain hammered the glass dome above us. The observatory door stood between us and the body, its compass emblem dark in the lamplight.

Kreel glanced at it. “We should move everyone downstairs.”

“We should keep everyone where I can see them.”

“You can’t interrogate us on a staircase.”

“I can if the alternative is letting someone alter the scene.”

“You’ve already altered it. You forced the door.”

“Yes. Because the alternative was leaving a dead man in a locked room.”

“Or a man who suffered a seizure.”

I looked at him. “You’re still arguing natural causes.”

“I’m arguing that we don’t know the cause.”

“That is different.”

“Is it?”

His mild patience reminded me of Daniel Wren’s supervisor, who had explained that documents could not be missing because the filing system had no provision for losing them. The more impossible the fact, the more confidently he had described the rules.

I went down first.

Orr had been moved from the library to a settee near the fire. Agnes had wrapped a towel around his injured head. His eyes were open, though unfocused.

“Is he conscious?” I asked.

“Enough to complain,” Agnes said.

Orr lifted a hand. “I heard the door.”

“Everyone heard it.”

“Not the door. Before that.”

I knelt beside him. “What did you hear?”

“Three clicks. Then something dragging.” He closed his eyes. “The clicks came from above. The dragging came after.”

“From the observatory?”

“I thought so.”

“You were in the library.”

“I know where I was.”

“Did you see anyone after the lights failed?”

“A shoulder. Passing the shelves.”

“Height? Clothing?”

“Dark coat. Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

“It was dark, Mara.”

He looked past me toward Kreel, who had taken up a position beside the fireplace, hands folded over his stick.

“I was struck from behind,” Orr continued. “I remember the case breaking and the bust coming down. After that, nothing.”

“Did you hear a voice?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

“What did it say?”

“Nothing. Breathing.”

“Male or female?”

“Close enough that I felt air against my ear.”

Agnes made a small sound. “You were concussed.”

“I was attacked.”

“No one disputes that,” I said. “But memory after a blow can be unreliable.”

“Then why ask?”

“Because unreliable isn’t useless.”

I left him with Agnes and called Celia into the morning room. I kept the door open. The others remained in the hall, close enough to hear raised voices.

Celia sat straight-backed, arms folded.

“When did you last see your father alive?” I asked.

“Before the blackout. Twenty minutes before, perhaps thirty.”

“You said he carried a folder.”

“A brown folder.”

“What was in it?”

“I don’t know.”

“You didn’t ask?”

“He told me not to look.”

“Your father told you not to look at a folder and you obeyed?”

“Our relationship was not simple.”

“What did he say?”

“He had work to do. He was going to the observatory.”

“Why?”

“He intended to examine papers there.”

“Which papers?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did he have the folder when he entered?”

“I didn’t see him enter.”

“Then how do you know he took it there?”

“I saw him walking toward the stairs.”

“Which stairs?”

“The suspended staircase.”

“Alone?”

“Yes.”

“Did he seem frightened?”

“He seemed determined.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

“Did you see the folder afterward?”

“No.”

“Did you enter the observatory tonight?”

“No. I was there yesterday with my father.”

“What did he show you?”

“The star map.”

“Any machinery?”

“My father showed people only what he wanted them to see.”

It was not an answer, but it told me she knew more than she intended.

“Do you know how the observatory door locks?”

“The key is usually kept on his ring.”

“Usually?”

“He had a duplicate once. I don’t know where it went.”

“Did you see the key tonight before we found it in his hand?”

“No.”

“Did you hear the door lock?”

“No.”

“Where were you during the blackout?”

“In the dining room.”

“Alone?”

“For part of it. Adrian was there, then he left. Agnes came through after the voice spoke.”

“Did you hear anything from above?”

“The house was making noises everywhere.”

That was true. It was also convenient.

“Did you kill your father?”

“No.”

“Did you help anyone reach him?”

“No.”

“Do you know of a hidden entrance to the observatory?”

She hesitated.

“I know the house has service spaces,” she said.

“Does everyone?”

“Not everyone.”

“Does your father?”

“He taught me how to find some of them. Not the observatory.”

Her fear was controlled, but real.

I sent her back and called Adrian.

He entered with his hands in his pockets, his posture loose and defensive.

“You heard the lock engage,” I said.

“I heard something engage.”

“Where?”

“On the landing below the observatory.”

“Why were you there?”

“I heard my father’s voice.”

“What did it say?”

“Nothing intelligible.”

“Earlier you said it sounded like him.”

“It did.”

“Calling whom?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did you answer?”

His jaw tightened. “I said, ‘Father?’”

“Did he respond?”

“No.”

“What happened next?”

“The lights came back. Then I heard the lock.”

“How long after the voice?”

“Seconds.”

“Did you see anyone on the stairs?”

“No.”

“Your father?”

“No.”

“Did you touch the observatory door?”

“No.”

“Did you knock?”

He stared at me. “I heard him calling. Then the house went silent. What would you have done?”

“I would have knocked.”

“Perhaps you should have been here earlier.”

The words landed harder than they deserved. I felt the old reflex—to defend my work, explain my decisions, make the timeline neat. That was how I had handled the Wren inquiry. Every contradiction became an inconvenience instead of a warning.

“What did you do after the lock?”

“I went downstairs.”

“Why?”

“I heard people shouting.”

“Who?”

“Celia. Maybe Agnes.”

“Maybe?”

“I was frightened.”

“Were you drunk?”

“No. Two glasses of wine.”

“Did your father know you were on the landing?”

“I don’t think so.”

“And you didn’t knock?”

He looked toward the stairs. “My father was inside.”

“And you left.”

“I heard the lock.”

“Which could have been the door.”

“I know what I heard.”

“Do you?”

He said nothing.

I sent him back to the hall.

Agnes remained standing when I called her. Her hands were clasped at her waist.

“You were caring for Orr during the blackout?”

“Yes.”

“In the library?”

“Yes.”

“The entire time?”

“Most of it. He was struck. I found him after the lights went out.”

“You said you were caring for him.”

“I was trying to.”

“Did you leave?”

“Only to fetch water.”

“From where?”

“The pantry.”

“How long?”

“A minute.”

“Long enough to reach the west passage?”

“No.”

“Did you hear the voice?”

“Yes.”

“Where did it come from?”

She looked at the walls. “Inside them.”

“Which wall?”

“I couldn’t say.”

“Did it say ‘Here’?”

“Yes.”

“Was it Vale’s voice?”

“No.”

She answered too quickly to be pretending certainty.

“Who could use the speaking tubes?”

“Kreel knows them.”

“Does Vale?”

“Vale designed them.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

She lowered her gaze. “Mr. Vale knew the house. Mr. Kreel knew how to make it work.”

The distinction was deliberate.

“Did you see Vale after dinner?”

“Yes. He came through the servants’ corridor.”

“When?”

“I don’t know. The clock there runs fast.”

“What was he carrying?”

“A folder.”

“Where was he going?”

“The stairs.”

“Did he speak to you?”

“He asked whether the observatory door had been checked.”

“For what?”

She pressed her lips together.

“Agnes.”

“He asked if the lower hinge was still reinforced.”

That was new.

“Did he seem afraid?”

“He seemed as if he had made up his mind.”

“About what?”

“He said, ‘Tonight, it ends.’”

The hall beyond the door had gone silent.

“Anything else?”

“He told me not to let Mr. Kreel near his study.”

Kreel’s stick stopped moving.

“Why?”

“I didn’t ask.”

“Did you obey?”

“No. I was with Mr. Orr when the lights failed.”

“Did you see Kreel during the blackout?”

“No.”

“Did you know where he was?”

“He said he was repairing the generator.”

“Did you believe him?”

Agnes looked toward the hall. “I believe what I can verify.”

I called Kreel last.

He did not sit until I gestured to the chair. The brass lamp had been left on the hall table, leaving his face flat and ordinary. Men who built elaborate lies rarely looked elaborate themselves.

“You were repairing the generator,” I said.

“Yes.”

“During the blackout.”

“Yes.”

“You left the dining room before the lights failed?”

“I was already in the west passage.”

“Why?”

“The generator had been unreliable all evening.”

“Who told you?”

“No one needed to. I heard it surge.”

“The coupling was loosened.”

“Then someone sabotaged it.”

“You found it.”

“I repaired it.”

“Did you use the maintenance hatch?”

“I used the passage.”

“So you entered a concealed route during the blackout.”

“A route intended for maintenance.”

“Does it lead toward the observatory?”

“Many routes lead toward many rooms.”

“Did you see Vale?”

“No.”

“Anyone?”

“No.”

“Did you hear a voice?”

“Everyone heard a voice.”

“Did you hear the observatory door lock?”

“I heard a door close.”

“Which door?”

“The observatory.”

“How do you know?”

“I was beneath it.”

The correction came too late.

“You were beneath the observatory?”

“In the west passage. It runs under part of the upper structure.”

“Why didn’t you say that before?”

“You asked whether I was repairing the generator.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the truth.”

He said it with polished calm.

“Could a person reach the observatory from that passage?”

“Not without dismantling a wall.”

“Could a mechanism do it?”

“A properly designed mechanism can do almost anything.”

“Was Blackwater properly designed?”

“It was designed by a man who valued effects over safety.”

“Did Vale know how to operate the observatory machinery?”

“Yes.”

“Did you?”

“I restored it.”

“Did you have access to the observatory before tonight?”

“For thirty years.”

“Did you have the key?”

“No.”

“Did you see Vale alive after dinner?”

“Only at dinner.”

“Then your account is no better than anyone else’s.”

“Perhaps not. But unlike the others, I’m not pretending the room proves murder.”

“Why are you eager for it to prove something else?”

“I’m eager for you to distinguish fact from theatricality.”

I looked toward the sealed door above us. The compass emblem pointed nowhere I trusted.

“Then let’s distinguish them.”

I addressed the household.

“Fact: Elias Vale was seen alive after dinner by Celia and Agnes, carrying a brown folder toward the upper stairs. Fact: Adrian heard a voice and then heard a mechanism engage near the observatory. Fact: Kreel was in a concealed maintenance passage during the blackout and did not initially mention it. Fact: no one admits seeing Vale cross the bridge. Fact: the observatory door was closed, the windows sealed, and the key was in Vale’s hand.”

No one spoke.

“These facts establish that Vale probably entered the observatory alive. They do not establish how he died, who killed him, or that anyone entered afterward.”

Celia looked toward the stairs. “But if no one entered—”

“Then the room was not entered conventionally.”

The answer frightened them more than certainty would have.

I continued, “No one goes upstairs. No one enters the study, library, generator room, or west passage. If you remember anything, tell me before you tell anyone else.”

“And if we don’t?” Kreel asked.

“Then I assume you are choosing what the house remembers for you.”

Behind him, somewhere inside the walls, a single metallic click sounded.

No one moved.

I wrote down the time, then the facts:

Vale alive when last observed. Cause unknown. Locked room unresolved. Conventional intruder unsupported.

The final line took longer.

Someone had built the room to lie.

I was no longer willing to let it speak first.

chapters.name: A Convenient Daughter
chapters.content:
## A Convenient Daughter

The click came again after I finished speaking.

It sounded from behind the walls, sharp enough to make everyone below the stairs look at someone else. Blackwater had taught its occupants to distrust one another without saying a word. The sound traveled through the stone, vanished beneath the suspended staircase, and seemed to return from somewhere above us.

“Back to the hall,” I said.

No one moved.

Celia stood beneath the staircase with her arms folded. Adrian leaned against the balustrade, wine staining one corner of his mouth. Agnes held a lamp in both hands, her knuckles pale around the brass handle. Kreel waited near the west corridor, as though the house had placed him there and he was content to remain part of its design.

“You heard me.”

Kreel glanced toward the sealed observatory door. “You’re treating a mechanism as though it has intention.”

“I’m treating the person operating it as though he does.”

“There’s no proof anyone is operating anything.”

“Then you won’t object to staying where I can see you.”

His mouth tightened. It was not quite a smile. “You’re giving orders in a private house.”

“There’s a dead man upstairs.”

“And no evidence yet that he was murdered.”

I looked at him. “You were the one who told me the door could close itself.”

“I told you the house contains mechanisms.”

“You also knew which hinge to force.”

“Because I restored it.”

“Exactly.”

For a moment, the only sound was rain striking the glass roof. Then Celia walked toward the central hall.

“Come on,” she said. “Let her search.”

Adrian straightened. “You can’t search private bedrooms without cause.”

“Your father is dead,” I said.

“And you think one of us killed him.”

“I think somebody did.”

“Who first?” Celia asked.

Her voice was calm, but her eyes were fixed on me.

“Yours.”

Adrian gave a short laugh. “That’s absurd. She had the strongest motive. She fought with Father over the development.”

“You owe money,” Celia said. “You threatened him at dinner.”

“I said I needed help.”

“You said you’d ruin him.”

“I said he couldn’t abandon us for a marina full of tourists.”

“You said you’d break his hands if he signed.”

Adrian’s face flushed. “You weren’t even in the room.”

“The walls carry sound.”

“Enough,” I said. “Celia, open the door.”

She looked at me for a moment, then crossed the hall. Kreel and Adrian followed. I had ordered everyone to remain together; neither man seemed inclined to obey, but neither wanted to be absent when the search began. Agnes came last, pausing beside Orr, who was being helped upright on the settee.

“Stay here,” I told her.

She nodded, though her gaze lingered on the dark west corridor.

Celia’s room was above the old conservatory. Its door opened with a reluctant scrape, as though the hinges had swollen in the damp. The room was spare: narrow bed, writing table, two chairs, wardrobe, and windows facing the sea. A charcoal sketch of Blackwater covered one wall. Seen from above, the house resembled a closed instrument, its wings folded around the central hall.

The storm made the windows tremble. Each gust pressed the curtains inward, then released them.

I stood in the doorway and let my eyes adjust.

“Where is the brown folder your father carried?” I asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Did you bring it here?”

“No.”

“Did you take it from him?”

“No.”

“Did you see where he took it?”

“He was walking toward the stairs. He said he had work to do.”

“You didn’t follow?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I was angry with him.”

“That has never stopped anyone from following someone they intend to kill.”

Her expression hardened. “If you want every ordinary act to sound criminal, you won’t need evidence.”

I entered the room. Adrian hovered at the threshold until I turned toward him.

“Everyone comes in or everyone stays out.”

He entered. Kreel remained outside.

“You too,” I said.

“I can see the room from here.”

“You can see the doorway. Come in.”

He did so with the air of a man indulging a child.

I searched the desk first. The drawers held stationery, a fountain pen, photographs, and property notices. Beneath the papers lay a brass key tied with blue thread.

“What does this open?”

“The conservatory.”

“Why was it under the papers?”

“Because I put it there.”

“Which is another word for hiding.”

“It’s another word for putting something somewhere I could find it.”

I held the key to the light. Its teeth were worn, but not recently. There was no grit or oil on it.

“Did anyone else know it was here?”

“No.”

“Your father?”

“I don’t know.”

“You put it there before or after dinner?”

“Before.”

“Why?”

“Because the conservatory door sticks. I needed the key.”

Adrian made a satisfied sound.

Celia turned on him. “Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“I’m enjoying not being the one in trouble.”

I moved to the wall sketch. Its frame was shallow and sealed with dust, but a clean line ran along the lower edge. I lifted the frame from its hook and examined the plaster behind it. No compartment. No displaced nails. Only a pale rectangle where the sketch had protected the wall from smoke and age.

The drawing itself showed the house’s east elevation. Celia had rendered the glass bridges as thin black strokes, but beneath them she had drawn the foundation as a series of heavy, uncertain lines.

“Did you make this?”

“Yes.”

“From memory?”

“From the original plans.”

“Which plans?”

“My mother’s.”

“Where are they?”

“Gone.”

“Destroyed?”

“Father took them.”

“Or you did?”

She looked at me. “You’ve already decided what I am.”

“No. I’m trying to decide what you know.”
